slides.say: Data Science from Scratch, lesson thirteen: sampling, and sampling bias.

slides.text: We rarely get data on everyone
slides.sub: Population: the whole group · Sample: the part you observe
slides.say: We rarely get data on every single person or transaction we care about. The whole group is called the population. The part we actually observe is the sample, and we use it to learn about the whole.

slides.text: A sample should look like the population
slides.say: A good sample looks like the population in the ways that matter. Then what's true in the sample is likely to be roughly true for everyone.

slides.text: Everyone has an equal chance of being picked
slides.sub: The simplest way to avoid picking favourites
slides.say: The simplest approach is a random sample, where every member of the population has an equal chance of being picked. That stops you, or your process, from choosing favourites.

slides.text: When some groups are more likely to be included
slides.sub: An online-only survey misses people who aren't online
slides.say: Sampling bias happens when some groups are more likely to end up in your data than others. For example, an online-only survey misses people who aren't online, so its results can't speak for them.

slides.text: You only see the cases that were caught
slides.sub: Fraud that slipped through never gets a label
slides.say: Fraud data has a classic version of this. Your labelled fraud cases are usually the ones that were caught. Fraud that slipped through often never gets a label, so your data can quietly over-represent the easy-to-catch kinds.

slides.text: Ask: who is missing from my data?
slides.say: So the takeaway: before you trust any result, ask who or what is missing from your data, and why.

summary: A sample is the part of a population you actually observe. Random sampling helps a sample represent the population; sampling bias happens when some groups are more likely to be included than others.
practice: Imagine a bank surveys customers only through its mobile app. Write down two groups of customers this survey might miss, and how that could skew the results.
